rationale: The book's core — that righteousness in Scripture's own usage denotes the doing of God's commandments (right-living), not a vague goodness nor a verdict merely received — is carried directly by texts that function as explicit definitions: Deuteronomy 6:25 ('it shall be our righteousness, if we observe to do all these commandments'), Psalm 119:172 ('all thy commandments are righteousness'), and 1 John 3:7, which is framed as a warning against precisely the deception the book targets ('let no man deceive you: he that doeth righteousness is righteous'). The garment elaboration is likewise anchored by Revelation 19:8, where the text itself defines the wedding linen as the dikaiōmata — the righteous acts — of the saints, a plural-active noun the ASV/ESV/NASB/NIV all render as deeds; the forensic reading depends heavily on the KJV's flattened 'righteousness of saints.' Crucially, the book does not evade the strongest counter-texts but re-derives them: Romans 4 is read through its own verse 4 definition of the excluded 'work' as a wage-claim of debt, with vv. 6-8 explaining the reckoning as forgiveness of sins plus faith counted as the right response; Philippians 3:9 is read as a contrast of source and claim ('mine own' by debt vs. 'of God by faith'), which vv. 12-16 support by immediately commanding walking by the rule attained; Isaiah 64:6 is shown to stain the doer, not the deed. The forensic counter-reading, to survive the supplied texts, must split righteousness into two barely-related senses (positional vs. practical) and read Rev 19:8, Deut 6:25, Ps 119:172, 1 John 3:7, Rev 22:14, and Rev 16:15 as a secondary sense — a larger unsupported step than the book's unified account, which still preserves grace as the mode of reception ('granted, then worn'; Eph 2:10; the linen 'given unto her'). No supplied text is explained by the counter that the book's core cannot explain without contradiction. Prior accepted premises on belief, faith, and love — each adjudicated as obedience-constitutive covenant responses — independently cohere with and reinforce this reading of the reckoning texts.
book_core_identification: Righteousness is the doing of God's commandments — right-living as substance, enacted conduct in conformity to God's revealed will — such that it is neither an undefined moral quality nor solely a forensic verdict received; it is granted by God in source (forgiveness, ordination of the works, the covenant covering) but is deeds in substance, symbolized as the garment of righteous acts worn.
book_secondary_elaborations: The garment/fine-linen symbol as righteousness performed (Rev 19:8 dikaiōmata; Job 29:14; Isa 61:10), with nakedness as its covenant-breach opposite
The covenant-clothing grammar of Ezekiel 16: covering first, then clothing of the covered; the garment as 'the covenant worn'
The bath/feet-washing distinction (John 13): baptism once, daily cleansing of the walk keeping the garment clean
The reading of Isaiah 64:6 as stain from the sinful doer rather than filth in obedience itself
The armor of God as God's own war-dress from Isaiah 59 lent to the believer, with the helmet as yeshuah/Christ covering the head
The fig-leaf covering as self-defined righteousness contrasted with God's blood-cost covering
God's own righteousness as Right-Living by definition since His ways are the measure (Deut 32:4; Ps 145:17)
strongest_counter_interpretation: The classic Protestant forensic/imputed reading: righteousness, in its decisive saving sense, is a legal status — the righteousness of God credited to the believer through faith apart from works (Rom 4:3-8; Rom 5:17-19; 2 Cor 5:21; Phil 3:9). On this view the garment imagery (Isa 61:10; Zech 3:4) pictures a righteousness bestowed and put on the sinner from outside, precisely not woven from his deeds; Isaiah 64:6 shows human righteous acts are disqualified as filthy rags; and texts like Deut 6:25, Ps 119:172, and 1 John 3:7 describe a secondary, practical righteousness (sanctification) that evidences but does not constitute the righteousness by which one stands before God.
counter_core_identification: Righteousness before God is fundamentally a declared and imputed status received by faith, not conduct performed; the doing of commandments is fruit and evidence of that status, never its substance.
material_core_denial: The counter denies that righteousness is in substance the doing of God's commandments, asserting instead that the righteousness that matters coram Deo is exclusively an alien, credited verdict — i.e., it affirms exactly what the book's entry rules out: 'a verdict only received.' Both identifications cannot be true of the same referent as the primary meaning.
counter_case: Romans 4:3-8: righteousness is 'counted' to the one who 'worketh not, but believeth,' language of crediting apart from deeds
Philippians 3:9: Paul renounces 'mine own righteousness, which is of the law' for one 'through the faith of Christ,' suggesting righteousness before God is categorically not law-keeping
2 Corinthians 5:21 and Romans 5:17-19: righteousness as something believers 'become' or receive as a 'gift' through one man's obedience, not their own
Isaiah 64:6: 'all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags' — human righteous deeds cannot constitute standing before God
Isaiah 61:10 and Zechariah 3:4: the robe of righteousness is bestowed by God on the unclean, imagery of covering from outside rather than conduct from within
Revelation 19:8 (KJV): 'the righteousness of saints' read as granted status — 'it was given unto her'
book_explanatory_advantages: Deuteronomy 6:25 and Psalm 119:172 are explicit scriptural definitions equating righteousness with commandment-keeping; the counter must demote them to a secondary sense with no textual signal of a sense-shift

1 John 3:7 is framed as an anti-deception warning ('let no man deceive you') that directly targets divorcing the status ('is righteous') from the doing ('doeth righteousness'), which the book's core predicts and the counter must soften

Revelation 19:8's own interpretive clause defines the linen as dikaiōmata — plural righteous acts — which the book reads at face value and the counter can sustain only through the KJV's narrowed rendering; the same verse's 'given unto her' is absorbed by the book via Eph 2:10 (deeds ordained, granted, then walked)

The book explains Romans 4 using Romans 4's own definitions: v. 4 defines the excluded work as a debt-claim, and vv. 6-8 gloss the reckoning as forgiveness of sins — God forgiving wrong-living and counting trusting faith as the right response, not renaming wrong-living right; the counter typically imports 'Christ's active obedience credited' into the passage, a step Romans 4 never states
Philippians 3:9's context (vv. 12-16: pressing on, 'walk by the same rule') supports the book's source-and-claim reading over a conduct-vs-status reading

Isaiah 64:6 read whole ('we are all as an unclean thing') locates the filth in the doer, not the deed — coherent with Rev 7:14 and Zech 3:4 where garments are washed, not discarded; the counter's 'obedience itself is filth' reading collides with Rev 3:4, Rev 16:15, Rev 22:14, and Jude 23, which command keeping garments undefiled

The wedding-garment parable's condemnation (Matt 22:11-13) and Rev 16:15's warning make the garment something the invited can lack or lose by conduct, which the book explains and a pure once-imputed-status reading strains to accommodate

The covenant-clothing sequence of Ezekiel 16 (covering, then clothing; skirt bearing the commandment-fringe of Num 15:39) supplies an Old Testament grammar for garment symbolism that matches the book's 'granted, then worn' structure

Consistency with accepted prior premises: belief, faith, and love were each adjudicated as covenant responses in which obedience is constitutive, so 'faith counted for righteousness' on those premises already contains right response rather than bare assent credited
counter_explanatory_advantages: It gives the most natural surface reading of the crediting language in Romans 4:5 ('to him that worketh not') and of the gift language in Romans 5:17
2 Corinthians 5:21's exchange formula ('made sin for us... that we might become the righteousness of God') fits an imputation frame readily and is only indirectly handled by the book
It preserves the strong Pauline polemic against boasting and works-confidence with a simpler mechanism (declaration) than the book's forgiveness-plus-right-response account
decisive_sources: Deuteronomy 6:25 — an explicit definitional statement: observing to do all the commandments 'shall be our righteousness'
1 John 3:7 — 'he that doeth righteousness is righteous,' framed as a warning against the opposite deception
Revelation 19:8 — the text's own gloss: the fine linen is the dikaiōmata (righteous acts) of the saints, given and then arrayed
Romans 4:4-8 — the passage's internal definition of the excluded work as a debt-claim and its gloss of reckoning as forgiveness, supporting the book's reading of the crediting texts
Ezekiel 16:8-13 with Numbers 15:39 — covenant covering carrying the commandment-fringe, grounding the garment-as-covenant-kept symbolism
Revelation 3:4, 16:15, 22:14 and Jude 23 — garments kept, defiled, or lost by conduct, inexplicable if the garment is a once-for-all forensic status only
unresolved_objections: 2 Corinthians 5:21 and Romans 5:17-19 are not directly exegeted in the supplied chapter; the imputation reading of these two texts retains some independent force even if it cannot overturn the definitional texts

The New Perspective construal of 'the righteousness of God' as God's own covenant faithfulness is partially convergent with the book (God going forth to do right, Isa 59) but its account of Paul's justification language is not adjudicated here
The book's claim that Rev 19:8's KJV rendering generated a 'long confusion' is a historical assertion about reception, not itself demonstrated from the sources

The precise mechanism by which faith is 'reckoned' as righteousness (right-response counted vs. status declared) remains a mechanism-level dispute the chapter argues but does not exhaustively settle for every Pauline text
